resource.name: Collecting Taxes Database - Administrative Data
resource.description:
USAID's Collecting Taxes Database (CTD) is a compilation of international statistics about taxation designed to provide policymakers, practitioners, and researchers with the means to conduct analysis on domestic revenue mobilization (DRM). It is part of a wider agenda of the international community to help countries strengthen their tax systems and mobilize domestic revenue.

The CTD includes information on tax performance and tax administration variables for 200 countries and territories. USAID plans to update the CTD annually.

The CTD comprises a set of 30 indicators divided into three main categories -- (1) Tax
Rates and Structure; (2) Tax Performance; and (3) Tax Administration -- and includes
information on 200 national tax systems. The tax administration indicators examine the main features of the revenue authority.

resource.name: Program Evaluation of USAID/Uganda SUSTAIN Activity: SUSTAIN Project Staff Data
resource.description:
USAID/Uganda’s Strengthening Uganda’s Systems for Treating AIDS Nationally (SUSTAIN) activity supports Uganda’s Ministry of Health (MOH) to strengthen quality and comprehensive HIV/AIDS care, prevention, laboratory and tuberculosis (TB) services at selected regional referral and district health care facilities in Uganda, as well as build the capacity of the public health system to sustain these services. SUSTAIN is a six­-year USAID­-funded activity launched in 2010 and implemented by University Research Co., LLC (URC). SUSTAIN is one of many PEPFAR-­funded activities to address the HIV/AIDS epidemic in Uganda. The main objective of the SUSTAIN program evaluation was to examine the activity’s methodology for achieving its
objectives in order to inform future USAID design work. USAID noted that URC had performed well on SUSTAIN, as evidenced by its activity reports, but wanted an evaluation of the approach used by SUSTAIN to inform future program designs. SUSTAIN implementation adapted to contextual changes in the Government of Uganda's (GoU) HIV/AIDS strategy responding to a spike in new infections and people living with HIV, and major shifts in PEPFAR policy.

resource.name: Cambodia Health Information Management System Data Demand and Information Use: Commune Council Dataset
resource.description:
This dataset solicits information about the respondents’ knowledge regarding the use and preparation of health data within the commune investment plan. It also asks the respondents to identify how they use health data and to what extent they understand the Cambodia Health Information Management System.

The overall objective of this study was to assess the current data use and information needs from Health Management Information System (HMIS) to support evidence based decision making among various health managers and information needs of other external health and non-health stakeholders at both National and Sub-National levels. The study was designed to assess the current data use; identify data requirements and highlight any existing barriers and constraints to data access for the purposes of decision-making and performance monitoring.

resource.name: USAID Forward, Maximize resources by leveraging commercial private capital_2010-2016
resource.description: This dataset contains the percent of program funds leveraging private capital through the DCA during the period 2010-2016, a part of the USAID Forward reform initiative that ran from 2010-2016.  USAID Forward improved the way that the Agency delivers foreign assistance by embracing new partnerships, investing in the catalytic role of innovation, and demanding a renewed focus on results.  In 2017, the Agency determined that the work advanced under USAID Forward had largely been institutionalized.  On this site, you will find the FY 2012-2016 data related to USAID Forward's three main areas of focus: 1) Deliver results on a meaningful scale through a strengthened USAID, 2) Promote sustainable development through high-impact partnerships and local solutions, and 3) Identify and scale up innovative, breakthrough solutions to intractable development challenges.  As of October 2017, we are no longer updating information, including collecting indicators, on this legacy effort.

resource.name: Haiti Sorghum Intercropping Sugarcane Aphid Study 2018-2019 - Mid-Season Dataset
resource.description: This dataset captures mid-season aphid counts.  It contains 1,080 rows and 7 columns.  Two experiments were conducted, one planted on 8/22/2018 (fall 2018) and another planted on 1/19/2019 (spring 2019), in Jonc-Labeille, Haiti. Three experimental treatments were compared: sorghum, sorghum intercropped with maize, and sorghum intercropped with pigeon pea. The sorghum variety was “Bout gode,” the maize variety was “Chicken corn,” and the pigeon pea was “Pwa kongo local.” A randomized complete block design experiment was used.

domain_metadata.value: Julien Beuzelin. 2023. Haiti Sorghum Intercropping Sugarcane Aphid Study 2018-2019 - Mid-Season Dataset. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/r4qq-5iwv.

This study provides some biological and ecological information about populations of sugarcane aphids on a cycle of crops grown in Les Cayes Haiti. It examines effects of growing sorghum as a sole crop or intercropped with other crops on the sugarcane aphid which is a pest of sorghum.

resource.name: Senegal USAID/PEPAM Ex-Post Evaluation Water Survey Data
resource.description:
The PEPAM/USAID Ex-Post Evaluation data were collected to assess the sustainability of the Millennium Water and Sanitation Program in Senegal (PEPAM/USAID – Programme d’Eau Potable et d’Assainissement du Millénaire au Sénégal). Implemented from 2009–2014 by Research Triangle Institute (RTI) and a consortium of partners, PEPAM aimed to improve sustainable access to water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) in four regions of Senegal.

The Senegal USAID/PEPAM Ex-Post evaluation Water Survey Data includes the water survey data collected as a part of the evaluation.  This data has also been merged with the applicable (if any) water point data associated with the survey respondents' village.

domain_metadata.value: Social Impact, ECODIT. 2020. Senegal USAID/PEPAM Ex-Post Evaluation Water Survey Data. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/r4wb-4esh.
Bureau for Resilience and Food Security

Social Impact has a detailed process for de-identifying evaluation datasets, which included removing identifying variables (names, contact information, gps points, etc) as well as recoding some variables to reduce the potential risk of respondent identification.  As a part of the internal review process, Social Impact's Institutional Review Board (IRB) has also reviewed the anonymization process for this data.
Data have been de-identified.  Direct identifiers have been removed and indirect identifiers have been recoded to reduce the potential risk of individual identification.

The data collected for the PEPAM/USAID Ex-post Evaluation derive from a single round of data collection in a sample of communities where PEPAM/USAID was implemented.  Though a wide variety of WASH-related variables are included, the sample was designed to be representative of project communities, but not necessarily of the regions or communes of Senegal more broadly.

resource.name: Baseline Study of Food for Peace Title II Development Food Assistance Program in Niger--Mother Pregnancy
resource.description: This dataset describes the behavior of the mothers during pregnancy as determined in the Baseline Study of Food for Peace Title II Development Food Assistance Program in the Maradi and Zinder regions in Niger.  It has 19 columns and 2,262 rows.   In fiscal year 2012, USAID's Office of Food for Peace (FFP) awarded funding to private voluntary organizations (PVOs) to design and implement a multi-year Title II development food assistance program in Niger. The main purpose of the Title II program is to improve long-term food security of chronically food insecure population in the target regions. FFP contracted a firm, ICF International to conduct a baseline study in targeted areas of the country prior to the start of the new program.  The purpose of the study was to assess the current status of key indicators, have a better understanding of prevailing conditions and perceptions of the population in the implementation areas, and serve as a point of comparison for future final evaluations.  Results would also be used to further refine program targeting and, where possible, to understand the relationship between variables to inform program design.  The study was conducted in 2013, while FFP expects to conduct final evaluations as close as possible to the end of the program five years later.

resource.name: Feed the Future Tanzania Mboga na Matunda Producer Survey 2018 - Module C Womens Diet
resource.description:
This dataset contains information on dietary diversity of female household members of producer beneficiaries included in the FY 18 producer survey.
This dataset is Module C of a data asset that contains data from the beneficiary based fiscal year 2018 annual results survey of smallholder producers assisted by the Feed the Future Tanzania - Mboga na Matunda Project. The project works to improve the livelihoods of horticultural farmers in the regions of Iringa, Morogoro, Songwe, Mbeya, and Zanzibar, and strengthen the market system throughout the ZOI. The survey sample was developed using a two-staged cluster design. In the first stage, 77 villages were selected for inclusion in the survey using the method of probability proportional to size based on beneficiary population data as recorded in FTFT-MnM's client database. In the second stage, 12 respondents were selected from each village. In total, 932 respondents were surveyed. The data is split into modules. Module A captures basic demographic data and landholdings. Module B captures information on the household members. Module C captures information on the dietary diversity of female household members. Modules D, E, F, G capture data on production of horticultural produce and associated costs, as well as information on sales. Module H captures information on access to finance.

This is a binary indicator of access to improved sanitation facilities. The variable is based on questions D05 and D06 following WHO and UNICEF classifications. Improved sanitation is classified as flush or pour toilets that are flushed to piped sewer systems, septic tanks, pit latrines, or unknown places. It also includes ventilated improved pit latrines, pit latrines with slabs, and composting toilets. Unimproved sanitation is flush toilets that flush to elsewhere, pit latrines without a slab open pit, bucket, hanging toilets, or no facilities, bush, field. All shared or public facilities are classified as unimproved.

The purpose of collecting these data was to examine farm expansion and labor markets in rural Tanzania. Data were collected in 8 rural districts of Tanzania: Mvomero, Kilombero, Njombe, Kiteto, Magu, Moshi Rural, Mkuranga and Liwale.

The data were collected through the Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Food Security Policy (FSP).

domain_metadata.value:
Examine the rate of land expansion of medium- and large-scale farms compared
to small scale farms, look at policy implications of consequent changes in
farm structure and the concentration of food production and marketed output;
Examine the pace of acquisition of agricultural land by medium- and
large-scale investors through de facto land administration policies; examine
the implication of such dynamics on rural youth land accessibility and out
migration in the context of customary tenure systems; assess the broader
effects of changing farm structure on the types of pace of non-farm
employment growth; understand the relationship between farm size and
efficiency, including the range of factors and policies that might condition
this relationship and specifically examine the impacts of large commercial
agricultural operations on the welfare of rural communities around them.
Examine the extent of land disputes and conflicts in rural Tanzania, their
causes, possible resolution mechanisms, and policy implications to land
investments in Tanzania as well as the implications of the formal and
informal land tenure systems in shaping incidence and intensity of land
dynamics.

resource.name: Program Evaluation of USAID/Uganda SUSTAIN Activity: HIV Clinic Staff Data
resource.description:
USAID/Uganda’s Strengthening Uganda’s Systems for Treating AIDS Nationally (SUSTAIN) activity supports Uganda’s Ministry of Health (MOH) to strengthen quality and comprehensive HIV/AIDS care, prevention, laboratory and tuberculosis (TB) services at selected regional referral and district health care facilities in Uganda, as well as build the capacity of the public health system to sustain these services. SUSTAIN is a six­-year USAID­-funded activity launched in 2010 and implemented by University Research Co., LLC (URC). SUSTAIN is one of many PEPFAR-­funded activities to address the HIV/AIDS epidemic in Uganda. The main objective of the SUSTAIN program evaluation was to examine the activity’s methodology for achieving its
objectives in order to inform future USAID design work. USAID noted that URC had performed well on SUSTAIN, as evidenced by its activity reports, but wanted an evaluation of the approach used by SUSTAIN to inform future program designs. SUSTAIN implementation adapted to contextual changes in the Government of Uganda's (GoU) HIV/AIDS strategy responding to a spike in new infections and people living with HIV, and major shifts in PEPFAR policy.

domain_metadata.value: President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR)
Panagora Group. 2020. Program Evaluation of USAID/Uganda SUSTAIN Activity: HIV Clinic Staff Data. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/s2xx-pr2j.
Although the evaluators did identify participants in the focus groups and key informant interviews, the data that could identify respondents was not included in any of the spreadsheets.

The dataset consists of recorded responses to a series of questions asked during key informant interviews (KII) or client focus groups regarding the delivery of HIV/AIDS related services. There are 11 spreadsheets, each recording the answers of a different set of actors in health service delivery: district health officers, focus groups comprised of clients (two spreadsheets), clinic staff, laboratory staff, implementing partners, lower level facility staff, Ministry of Health staff, regional referral hospital staff, SUSTAIN project staff, and USAID staff.

resource.name: Ghana Early Grade Math Pilot Impact Evaluation: Baseline Head Teacher Dataset
resource.description: The Early Grade Math Pilot program in Ghana, implemented under the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) Partnership for Education Learning Activity, was evaluated with an independent randomized controlled trial between 2017 and 2018. This data asset contains the two waves of data collected in Ghana during this time period. This dataset contains survey head teacher data from the activity baseline.

domain_metadata.value: Social Impact. 2023. Ghana Early Grade Math Pilot Impact Evaluation: Baseline Head Teacher Dataset. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/s6bm-82r7.

All data sets in this data asset have been comprehensively anonymized according to Social Impact procedures. Anonymization procedures included removing direct identifiers and removing or recoding indirect identifiers. These datasets were subsequently reviewed and approved for dissemination by Social Impact's internal Institutional Review Board.

This data asset contains detailed data from a total of four survey instruments, one classroom observation tool, and pupil scores on the EGRA and GENA assessments. This data was collected from 120 schools, 240 teachers, and 4,800 pupils. As such, this data asset contains substantial information regarding primary education in Ghana.

resource.name: Mini Survey Data for the Advancing National Integration in Georgia Activity Mid-term Performance Evaluation
resource.description: During the course of an evaluation, the Evaluation Team conducted a mini-survey among the members of the 13 youth centers supported under a program to promote integration of diverse population groups into Georgian society.  The ANI program is implemented by a Georgian organization, the United Nations Association of Georgia (UNAG).  The survey is based on a random sample of 160 respondents selected proportional to their distribution among members based on their ethnicity and gender.

resource.name: Early Grade Reading Activity Malawi 2013 EGRA Baseline
resource.description:
The Malawi Early Grade Reading Activity (MEGRA) is a multifaceted educational development approach intended to enable sustained literacy among children, promote a literate community, and help the country increase economic growth and reduce poverty. The USAID/Malawi funded program was implemented starting August of 2013, by RTI (Research Triangle Institute) International. The MEGRA educational program was implemented alongside a Feed the Future project called Integrating Nutrition in Value Chains (INVC) and a Global Health Initiative project called Support for Service Delivery Integration (SSDI), both of which were also expected to affect the success of learners in school. Through this interconnected strategy, USAID/Malawi aimed to have a greater impact on outcomes of interest (such as learning reading scores) than would otherwise be possible through one project alone. The key elements of the MEGRA reading intervention involved:

•	Conduct teacher training, including practicums

•	Provide scripted lesson plans to teachers

•	Provide in-service teacher support and mentoring (or coaching)

•	Provide rewards for high-performing teachers and schools

•	Develop and distribute books, story cards, letter cards, and bookshelves

•	Organize reading fairs and other events to engage parents, caregivers, and the community in learner learning

•	Invite parents to participate in their learners’ classrooms and/or become engaged in extracurricular activities

•	Ensure a supportive policy environment by attending the Basic Education Technical Working Group and writing Memorandums of Understanding (MOUs) to gain necessary Ministry of Education, Science, and Technology(MoEST) support and buy-in

•	Facilitate the extension of school instructional time

In order to test possible complementary or multiplier effects of the MEGRA reading intervention and the INVC and SSDI activities, all three interventions were implemented in and evaluated for four distinct treatment levels:

•	Treatment Level 1: Three focus districts (Balaka, Machinga, and Lilongwe Rural) that provide an opportunity to evaluate the impact of a fully-integrated development approach with multiple activities across sectors, including MEGRA, INVC, and SSDI, on early grade reading outcomes.

•	Treatment Level 2: The district (Salima) where MEGRA overlaps with only the SSDI intervention. This serves as a test ground for the hypothesis that synergies between education and health initiatives catalyze changes that are greater than the sum of their parts.

•	Treatment Level 3: The district (Ntcheu) where MEGRA overlaps with only the INVC intervention. This serves as a test ground for the development hypothesis that synergies between education and agricultural livelihood and nutrition initiatives catalyze changes that are greater than the sum of their parts.

•	Treatment Level 4: Five districts (Blantyre Rural, Mzimba North, Ntchisi, Thyolo, and Zomba Rural) that only receive the MEGRA initiative. These districts are used to test the MEGRA theory of change that education support leads to improved literacy and general education outcomes.

MEGRA was implemented at the zonal level, at baseline in 2013, where zones were randomly selected in each of the four levels to implement the MEGRA intervention (taking into account areas where INVC and SSDI were already working). However, since INVC and SSDI were not randomly assigned at baseline, the evaluation can only be able to determine whether EGRA is better than no EGRA and whether EGRA plus INVC and SSDI is better than no treatment.

While MEGRA expected to include both treatment and comparison schools in each district at each level, at baseline, it was unable to because the SSDI and INVC activities were already underway. As such, the program found that in the Level 2 district, Salima, it was impossible to select comparison zones that were not already contaminated with the SSDI intervention because SSDI was already work

Kamath-Rayne, Adrien Lokangaka, Casey Lowman, Eric Mafuta, Helge Myklebust, Tracy Nolen, Janna Patterson, Antoinette Tshefu, Carl Bose, Sara K. Berkelhamer

Please see the USAID Data Services DDL Variable Manipulation Overview,  https://data.usaid.gov/api/views/xw2i-z7hr/files/de8f1fd7-1803-43bf-9a5a-de5f67a57ccb, noting the risk mitigation techniques implemented in some data assets on the DDL, as well as examples of the impact of these techniques on the data.

In 2015, approximately 2.6 million pregnancies reportedly ended in stillbirths; 98% occurred in low and lower-middle income countries (LMICs). Nearly one-half of stillbirths were classified as fresh stillbirths, indicating that the fetus died during the intrapartum period. Typically, the diagnosis of a stillbirth was made because the newborn did not breathe following birth. Yet many of these non-breathing newborns classified as stillborn have a heart rate (HR) and are actually live born. The effect of a low-cost monitor for measuring HR on newborn survival is unknown. Knowledge of HR during newborn resuscitation might also result in administration of appropriate interventions, and improvement in outcomes. Helping Babies Breathe (HBB), a resuscitation algorithm developed by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), is widely accepted as the standard of care for newborn resuscitation in LMICs. In keeping with ILCOR recommendations that HR be measured during newborn resuscitation, HBB calls for heart rate assessment after one minute of positive-pressure ventilation with good chest movement (or sooner if there is a helper who can palpate/auscultate HR). However, given the frequent reality of a single provider attending deliveries in LMICs, as well as the currently available methods for assessing HR (i.e. palpation or auscultation), assessment of HR is challenging to perform without delaying or stopping the provision of other life-saving interventions such as bag and mask ventilation.  Furthermore, the most accurate method of HR assessment at birth is an electrocardiogram, which is not widely available in LMICs. NeoBeat is a low-cost alternative to continuously monitor HR that can guide resuscitation in these settings.

resource.name: Feed the Future Senegal: Yaajeende Women's Data
resource.description:
The purpose of this study is to evaluate the impact that the Feed the Future Nutrition-led Agriculture Project for Food Security in Senegal (known as "Yaajeende") has had on reducing malnutrition and poverty in its intervention area.

This report details the findings, conclusions and recommendations of a mixed-methods quasi-experimental final impact evaluation (FIE) of the United States Agency for International Development’s (USAID) $50 million, seven-year Feed the Future Nutrition-Led Agriculture Project for Food Security in Senegal, known as “Yaajeende.” The National Cooperative Business Association’s Cooperative League of the USA (NCBA CLUSA) implemented the project. To combat poverty and child malnutrition, Yaajeende sought to accelerate the participation of the very poor in rural economic growth and improve the four dimensions of food security: availability, access, utilization and stability. Yaajeende worked in 790 villages across 49 municipalities (“communes” in French) and nine departments in the Matam, Tambacounda, Kédougou and Kolda regions. The project’s implementation period was November 1, 2010, to September 30, 2017.

The FIE aims to provide USAID with an evidence base on the impacts of the nutrition-led agriculture (NLA) approach that the project utilized on its key objectives, including reduced poverty and malnutrition. The findings are expected to provide accountability and learning value to USAID, including both the Senegal Mission and USAID/Feed the Future. Additional stakeholders include the Government of Senegal, implementing partners and other agencies, donors and practitioners active in nutrition, health, agriculture and integrated sectors.

domain_metadata.value: Field trials on nitrogen and zinc fertilization of wheat in three provinces of Afghanistan (Herat, Kabul and Nangarhar) during the 2019-20 season. One of 20+ trials implemented during 2018/19, 2019/20, and 2020/21 under the USAID-funded Grain Research and Innovation (GRAIN) project implemented by Michigan State University, in partnership with partnership with Afghanistan’s Ministry of Agriculture, Irrigation, and Livestock (MAIL), the Agricultural Research Institute of Afghanistan (ARIA), the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA), and the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center (CIMMYT).
Bureau for Development, Democracy, and Innovation

Data from these agronomic trials were intended to serve as key information for preparing updated best-practice recommendations to wheat farmers in the major wheat-growing zones of Afghanistan. GRAIN project reports contain a preliminary analysis, but more thorough analysis could help refine the recommendations.

resource.name: Agricultural Land Dynamics and Land Policy in Rural Tanzania 2016: Off-farm Income Dataset
resource.description:
This dataset contains information about household income earned outside the farm business. The table can be combined with other datasets in this data asset using the 'hhid' column.

The purpose of collecting these data was to examine farm expansion and labor markets in rural Tanzania. Data were collected in 8 rural districts of Tanzania: Mvomero, Kilombero, Njombe, Kiteto, Magu, Moshi Rural, Mkuranga and Liwale.

The data were collected through the Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Food Security Policy (FSP).

Examine the rate of land expansion of medium- and large-scale farms compared
to small scale farms, look at policy implications of consequent changes in
farm structure and the concentration of food production and marketed output;
Examine the pace of acquisition of agricultural land by medium- and
large-scale investors through de facto land administration policies; examine
the implication of such dynamics on rural youth land accessibility and out
migration in the context of customary tenure systems; assess the broader
effects of changing farm structure on the types of pace of non-farm
employment growth; understand the relationship between farm size and
efficiency, including the range of factors and policies that might condition
this relationship and specifically examine the impacts of large commercial
agricultural operations on the welfare of rural communities around them.
Examine the extent of land disputes and conflicts in rural Tanzania, their
causes, possible resolution mechanisms, and policy implications to land
investments in Tanzania as well as the implications of the formal and
informal land tenure systems in shaping incidence and intensity of land
dynamics.

All GPS locations are rounded to 2 decimal places (accuracy of about 1 km) to protect sensitive sampling sites related to wildlife. Direct and indirect identifiers have been removed from human data using HIPAA Privacy Rule guidance and human data are aggregated and summarized to further protect individuals sampled.

This data includes both a wide range of variables and rare and unique variables related to known and novel viruses, including where and in what species they were found. Data were collected in Africa and Asia in communities with high-risk wildlife contact and includes variables that can inform on risk associated with zoonotic pathogen transmission and potential targets for intervention to minimize risk of pathogen spillover.

USAID Data Services identified variables within the asset that present privacy risk (key variables) and applied the following techniques: a 3-anonymity technique on categorical key variables, such as sex, occupation, business size and location. In order to reach the 3 - anonymity threshold, USAID Data Services recoded some variables, aggregated others and suppressed values that increased the risk of re-identification. Doing so, reduces the precision of the cells, while preserving statistical utility. 3-Anonymity mitigates risk on key categorical variables in a combined way. The names, phone numbers, and emails have been removed from the FFSWE datasets.

The FFSWE dataset details the support the program provided to all beneficiaries, whether they attended trainings, received technical assistance, or attended outreach events. The data reflects the impacts projects can have in Mali.

resource.description: The survey interviewed 254 retailer shops in 10 sub-cities of Addis Ababa. 30 supermarkets, 20 mini-markets, 100 regular shops, 80 dairy shops and 24 open market shops selling dairy products were interviewed. resource.name: Comprehensive African Agriculture Development Program (CAADP): Level 2 Indicators
resource.description: The Comprehensive African Agriculture Development Program (CAADP) was designed to promote interventions that best respond to the recognized precarious situation of African agriculture. Its focused goals are (a) extending the area under sustainable land management and reliable water control systems; (b) improving rural infrastructure and trade-related capacities for improved market access; and (c) increasing food supply and reducing hunger. The CAADP also pays attention to emergencies and disasters that require food and agricultural responses or safety nets.

resource.name: Malawi Baseline Impact Evaluation: Roster
resource.description:
Feed the Future initiative in Malawi is committed to improving food security and nutrition in farming households while reducing rural poverty through an agriculture-­led, integrated economic growth, nutrition, and natural resource management strategy. The goal of the impact evaluation is to determine whether integrating nutrition interventions
alongside agricultural value chain interventions will contribute to a greater reduction in malnutrition among children under 3 years of age, compared to nutrition improvements anticipated from stand-­alone value chain activities.

The main objectives are to enable USAID missions to meet the performance monitoring requirements of Feed the Future and maximize the use and benefits of data collected; provide high-­quality empirical evidence to inform program design and investment decisions that will promote sustainable food security; ensure timely availability of high­quality data for use in monitoring performance and evaluating impacts of the Feed the Future initiative; and facilitate accountability and learning about which Feed the Future interventions work best, under what conditions, and at what cost.

resource.name: Community Resilience Activity (CRA) Safe Charity Assessment: Phase 1 Farmer Leaders Data
resource.description:
The United States Agency for International Development (USAID)/Pakistan-funded Safe Charity campaign seeks to reduce financial support to violent extremist groups by educating those who give charity about how to direct their charity to safe recipients in Multan and Karachi. In Multan, the campaign trained influential farmers to disseminate safe charity messages to other farmers; and chambers of commerce and industry, trade and marketing associations, and the Rotary Club to reach the business community. In Karachi, the campaign engaged community youth centers to disseminate messages. The campaign timed its activities to align with common periods of charitable giving, namely Ramazan, Eid ul-Fitr, and Eid ul-Azha. 

These surveys established a baseline of current knowledge and practices with respect to safe charity in Multan and Karachi during each giving period and identified changes in knowledge and practices that could be plausibly linked to the safe charity campaign.

domain_tags: institute of social and policy sciences

domain_metadata.value: Management Systems International (MSI). 2020. Community Resilience Activity (CRA) Safe Charity Assessment: Phase 1 Farmer Leaders Data. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/t86q-3w5n.

The assessment conducted structured surveys of farmer and business communities in Multan and of participants of community youth center activities in Karachi. The assessment team collected survey data in two phases, each phase aligning with one of two selected periods of charitable and corresponding safe charity activities. Phase I aligned with activities relating to charitable giving during Ramazan and Eid ul-Fitr and collected data on decision-making patterns, knowledge, attitudes, and behavior with respect to the giving of zakat and fitrana during that period. Phase II aligned with activities relating to charitable giving during Eid ul-Azha and collected data on similar topics with respect to the giving of animal hides. The Phase II sample consisted primarily of individuals who had also participated in the Phase I survey. The primary limitation to the data from the Phase I survey was a snowball sampling approach to identifying survey respondents who had been exposed to safe charity messaging. For example, the survey team relied on farmer leaders, who had directly engaged with the safe charity campaign, to identify other members of farmer communities with knowledge of safe charity activities. While it was necessary to include “secondary” farmers in the survey sample to assess the reach of safe charity messaging within target communities, the survey team could not guarantee that secondary farmers had participated in safe charity activities or been exposed to safe charity messaging. Furthermore, there is a high likelihood of a selection bias in farmer leader referrals. To control for this bias, the survey team identified enough secondary farmers to create a secondary sampling frame, from which respondents could be randomly selected. The primary limitation to the survey of members of the business community was lack of familiarity with the safe charity campaign, particularly among corporate businesses. This may have been due to challenges identifying knowledgeable individuals within corporate businesses, lower levels of engagement between corporate businesses and their respective chambers of commerce, or characteristics of the corporate engagement strategy of the safe charity campaign.  Whereas the Phase I surveys focused on the giving of zakat and fitrana, the Phase II survey focused specifically on safe charity practices for the giving of qurbani. Phase II included only farmers and excluded the business community and Karachi youth center participants. The survey team employed a longitudinal design, surveying the same farmers who participated in Phase I. By surveying the same respondents, the assessment team examined layered (or repeated) exposure to safe charity activities and compared perceptions around different types of giving. However, given the unique circumstances and distinct forms of charity common to each charitable giving period, differences in behavior between Phase I and II should not be construed as change in behavior attributable to the safe charity campaign.

All unique individual identifiers, including names, addresses, and phone numbers of respondents, as well as names of data collection and processing teams, have been removed from the CRA Safe Charity study dataset and omitted from the final report. A unique identification code has been assigned to each survey respondent, reflecting the respondent’s geographic location (city), type of respondent (direct/indirect, farmers/businessman/workshop participants) and sex. The dataset does include information pertaining to respondents’ sex, educational attainment, religion, employment status, and income, which are important variables to explain variation in responses. These variables, however, together do not provide sufficient information to identify individual respondents.

The assessment team, led by MSI and the Institute of Social and Policy Sciences (I-SAPS), conducted structured surveys of farmer and business communities in Multan and of participants of community youth center activities in Karachi. The assessment team collected survey data in two phases, each phase aligning with one of two selected periods of charitable and corresponding safe charity activities. Phase I, which took place in August 2018, aligned with activities relating to charitable giving during Ramazan and Eid ul-Fitr and collected data on decision-making patterns, knowledge, attitudes, and behavior with respect to the giving of zakat and fitrana during that period. Phase II, which took place in October 2018, aligned with activities relating to charitable giving during Eid ul-Azha and collected data on similar topics with respect to the giving of animal hides. The Phase II sample consisted primarily of individuals who had also participated in the Phase I survey. Phase I included three surveys, each targeting a unique respondent group. In Multan, the assessment team selected a random sample of 124 farmer “leaders” from 500 farmers in 11 union councils who were directly engaged by the safe charity campaign. Farmer leaders were pre-identified influential members of their communities, tasked with disseminating information to other farmers and community members through community gatherings, sensitization sessions, and other activities and events. The sample of farmer leaders was stratified by gender and union council. With assistance from farmer leaders, the assessment team then used a snowball approach to identify a sampling frame of at least 500 “secondary” farmers, or members of target communities who participated in community gatherings, sensitizations sessions, and other activities and events sponsored by the safe charity campaign. Using this sampling frame, the assessment team selected a random sample of 150 secondary farmers, also stratified by gender and union council. The assessment team conducted a second Phase I survey of members of chambers of commerce and industry in Multan. The team randomly selected 150 businesses—120 members (40 corporate members and 80 associate members) of the Multan Chamber of Commerce and Industry (MCCI), whose total membership in Multan was approximately 1,000 businesses at the time of the survey; and 30 businesses from the Women Chamber of Commerce and Industry Multan (WCCIM), whose total membership in Multan was approximately 140 businesses at the time of the survey. The assessment team conducted a third Phase I survey of all 103 participants of safe charity poster workshops conducted at Azm-e-Naujawan (AeN) community youth centers. The campaign expected another 850 community members to attend AeN safe charity poster exhibits. Through AeN center staff and poster workshop participants, the assessment team used a snowball approach to identify a sampling frame of approximately 400 visitors to the poster exhibitions. From this sampling frame, the assessment team selected a random sample of 121 exhibit visitors, stratified by gender. As with secondary farmers, the snowball approach to identifying secondary participants could not ensure activity participation or exposure to safe charity messaging, and may have been subject to a selection bias. The Phase II survey focused solely on farmer leaders and secondary farmers in Multan. During Phase II, the assessment team surveyed 124 farmer leaders, 112 of whom were surveyed in Phase I and 12 of whom were new respondents who replaced farmers that could not be reached or who were unable to participate. Similarly, the assessment team surveyed 152 secondary farmers, 131 of whom were also surveyed in Phase 1, and 21 of whom were new respondents who replaced farmers that could not be reached or who were unable to participate. Together, these surveys provide a comprehensive snapshot of how people in these communities give charity and the role that the risk of giving to violent extremist groups plays in charitable decision-making. The surveys captured three types of information. First, they probed how people give charity, including frequency of giving, type of giving, who in the household makes charitable giving decisions, why people give charity, and factors determining to whom people give charity. Second, the surveys probed people’s knowledge of the risk of giving to violent extremist groups, where people obtain information about safe charity, and how this knowledge affects decision-making. Third, the surveys probed participation in safe charity activities and the effect of this participation on knowledge and behaviors, including further dissemination of safe charity messaging. The survey data can be disaggregated by gender, age, income, religion, and respondent type, as well as period of charitable giving. The two phases of data collection provide important insights into how hyperlocal conditions of place and time affect charitable decision-making and knowledge and practice of safe charity. The survey team employed a longitudinal design, surveying the same farmers who participated in Phase I. By surveying the same respondents, the assessment team examined layered (or repeated) exposure to safe charity activities and compared perceptions around different types of giving. However, given the unique circumstances and distinct forms of charity common to each charitable giving period, differences in behavior between Phase I and II should not be construed as change in behavior attributable to the safe charity campaign. The surveys are supplemented by in-depth individual and group interviews with primary and secondary safe charity participants.

resource.name: Impact Surveys for Smallholder Customers of Agricultural technologies in Kenya and Mozambique as Part of the Feed the Future Initiative- Data
resource.description: The Feed the Future Partnering for Innovation (FTF-P4I) initiative is a USAID-funded program that helps commercialize agricultural innovations in smallholder markets by supporting public-private partnerships to meet food security objectives.  FTF-P4I requires private sector subawardees to report on proprietary business and sales data rather than collect farmer-level data, and when necessary program staff then use this data in combination with assumptions around product usage to calculate specific indicators such as the number of farmers impacted by program activities or the number of hectares under improved technologies or management practices.  FTF-P4I then confirms farmer-level impact with additional field surveys, especially for subawardees with significant potential impact on women or with sales to farmers through third party distributors.  These measures guarantee greater data quality of both sales data and assumptions used to calculate indicators, such as the number of farmers applying improved technologies, as well as promote better precision on farmer-level impact and impact on women.  The submitted dataset includes the results of seven subawardees located in Kenya (Surehatch, AATF) and Mozambique (BOM, iDE, NCBA CLUSA, EMCL).

resource.name: Feed the Future Tanzania Mboga na Matunda Private Sector Survey 2019 - Module C Product
resource.description: This data asset contains data from the beneficiary based fiscal year 2019 annual results survey of private sector firms assisted by the Feed the Future Tanzania - Mboga na Matunda Project. The project works to improve the livelihoods of horticultural farmers in the regions of Iringa, Morogoro, Songwe, Mbeya, and Zanzibar, and strengthen the market system throughout the ZOI. The survey sample was developed using one level of stratification, firm type. Firms were selected from five different categories: Processor, Buyer, Local input supplier, Regional input supplier, Finance provider, and Other service provider. In total, 321 firms were surveyed. The data is split into modules. Module A captures basic identifying data on the firm. Module B captures information on the proprietors. Modules C, D, E, F, G and H capture data on sales of products and services. Module I captures information on business practices. Module J captures information on production costs. Module K captures information on access to finance.

resource.name: Haiti Sorghum Intercropping Sugarcane Aphid Study 2018-2019 - Late Season Dataset
resource.description: This dataset captures late season aphid counts.  It contains 1,080 rows and 8 columns.  Two experiments were conducted, one planted on 8/22/2018 (fall 2018) and another planted on 1/19/2019 (spring 2019), in Jonc-Labeille, Haiti. Three experimental treatments were compared: sorghum, sorghum intercropped with maize, and sorghum intercropped with pigeon pea. The sorghum variety was “Bout gode,” the maize variety was “Chicken corn,” and the pigeon pea was “Pwa kongo local.” A randomized complete block design experiment was used.

domain_metadata.value: Julien Beuzelin. 2023. Haiti Sorghum Intercropping Sugarcane Aphid Study 2018-2019 - Late Season Dataset. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/tjj9-6i9f.

This study provides some biological and ecological information about populations of sugarcane aphids on a cycle of crops grown in Les Cayes Haiti. It examines effects of growing sorghum as a sole crop or intercropped with other crops on the sugarcane aphid which is a pest of sorghum.

resource.name: Haiti Rice Sheath Blight 2018 - Rhizosphere Disease Rating Dataset
resource.description: This dataset captures data about rice plants treated with Rhizoctonia solani (R. Solani) inoculation. It contains 32 rows and 34 columns. The research falls within the field of biological control of plant diseases. Bacteria isolated from rice plants had been screened for their antagonistic activity against Rhizoctonia solani (R. solani), the rice sheath disease pathogen. The data reported contain the inhibition zone resulting from the antagonistic interaction of the bacteria and R. solani.  This experiment was performed by a USAID funded graduate student, Jhonson Leonard, in the laboratory of Dr. Jong Hyun Ham, located in the Department of Plant Pathology at the University of Louisiana.

domain_metadata.value: Dr. Jong Hyun Ham. 2021. Haiti Rice Sheath Blight 2018 - Rhizosphere Disease Rating Dataset. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/tkwj-r2qt.

This basic research data could be used to help individuals or organizations trying to find biological information about the rice sheath disease pathogen .  It looks at biological control approaches to disease control and the types of organisms associated with the rhizophere of rice plants with and without silica treatment.

resource.name: Malawi Baseline Impact Evaluation: Women's Data
resource.description:
Feed the Future initiative in Malawi is committed to improving food security and nutrition in farming households while reducing rural poverty through an agriculture-­led, integrated economic growth, nutrition, and natural resource management strategy. The goal of the impact evaluation is to determine whether integrating nutrition interventions
alongside agricultural value chain interventions will contribute to a greater reduction in malnutrition among children under 3 years of age, compared to nutrition improvements anticipated from stand-­alone value chain activities.

The main objectives are to enable USAID missions to meet the performance monitoring requirements of Feed the Future and maximize the use and benefits of data collected; provide high-­quality empirical evidence to inform program design and investment decisions that will promote sustainable food security; ensure timely availability of high­quality data for use in monitoring performance and evaluating impacts of the Feed the Future initiative; and facilitate accountability and learning about which Feed the Future interventions work best, under what conditions, and at what cost.

Doing so reduces the precision of the cells, while preserving statistical utility. 3-anonymity mitigates risk on key categorical variables in a combined way.

resource.name: Rift Valley Fever Innovation Lab: RVFV vaccine reassortment data -Tetsuro
resource.description:
Risk analysis of inter-species reassortment through a Rift Valley fever phlebovirus MP-12 vaccine strain

This study thus aimed to characterize the occurrence of genetic reassortment between the MP-12 strain and bunyavirus species closely related to RVFV. The Arumowot virus (AMTV) and Gouleako goukovirus (GOLV), are transmitted by mosquitoes in Africa. The results of this study showed that GOLV does not form detectable reassortant strains with the MP-12 strain in co-infected C6/36 cells. The AMTV also did not form any reassortant strains with MP-12 strain in co-infected C6/36 cells, due to the incompatibility among N, L, and Gn/Gc proteins. A lack of reassortant formation could be due to a functional incompatibility of N and L proteins derived from heterologous species, and due to a lack of packaging via heterologous Gn/Gc proteins. The MP-12 strain did, however, randomly exchange L-, M-, and S-segments with a genetic variant strain, rMP12-GM50, in culture cells. The MP-12 strain is thus unlikely to form any reassortant strains with AMTV or GOLV in nature. The supporting data for these observations are as follows:

resource.name: Baseline Study of Food for Peace Title II Development Food Assistance Program in Karamoja, Uganda--Household Description
resource.description: This dataset describes the households and its members surveyed as part of the Baseline Study of Food for Peace Title II Development Food Assistance Program in Karamoja,  Uganda.  This dataset contains data from Module A of the questionnaire and has 35 columns and 29,935 rows.  In fiscal year 2012, USAID's Office of Food for Peace (FFP) awarded funding to private voluntary organizations (PVOs) to design and implement a multi-year Title II development food assistance program in Uganda.  The main purpose of the Title II program is to improve long-term food security of chronically food insecure population in the target regions.  FFP contracted a firm, ICF International to conduct a baseline study in targeted areas of the country prior to the start of the new program.  The purpose of the study was to assess the current status of key indicators, have a better understanding of prevailing conditions and perceptions of the population in the implementation areas, and serve as a point of comparison for future final evaluations.  Results would also be used to further refine program targeting and, where possible, to understand the relationship between variables to inform program design.  The study was conducted in 2013, while FFP expects to conduct final evaluations as close as possible to the end of the program five years later.  The data asset is comprised of six datasets: 1) a description of all members of the households surveyed, 2) data on maternal health and sanitation practices, 3) data about the children in the household, 4) data describing the agricultural practices of the household, 5) data describing the food consumption of the household (broken into 4 smaller spreadsheets), and 6) and a description of the weights that should be applied during the analysis of the other datasets.

resource.name: Farm Plots Survey for Agriculture for Children's Empowerment (ACE) in Liberia- Household Member Baseline Dataset
resource.description:
The STRIVE project, funded by USAID's Displaced Children and Orphans Fund (DCOF) and managed by FHI 360, used market-led economic strengthening initiatives to improve the well-being of vulnerable children. Through STRIVE, ACDI/VOCA  implemented the Agriculture for Children’s Empowerment (ACE) Project in Liberia, which is founded on the premise that increased household economic security will stimulate more consistent investments in children’s well being via longer term social investments in education and nutrition.  ACE’s primary focus was on the horticulture value chain (VC) — the production and marketing of vegetables by smallholder farmers in Montserrado, Bong, and Nimba counties of Liberia. ACE also strengthened smallholder rice farming to increase household food security using a market-sensitive approach to rice seed lending and cultivation.

This dataset contains information about the members of each household surveyed.

resource.name: Institutional Capacity Baseline and Endline Measures - Climate Smart, Low Carbon Cities (CSLCC) Program
resource.description:
This data asset contains baseline and endline measures of key institutional partners participating in the Climate Smart, Low Carbon Cities (CSLCC) program. In the begining of the program, the CSLCC team identified technical expertise and stakeholder engagement as core areas of capacity improvement for each city’s local government and technical partners. The baseline assessment was conducted in 2016 through semi-structured and key informant interviews with the main partners in each city. After the interview, the CSLCC team rated each city partner per the capacity areas identified by using the Skill Set Inventory toolkit. The endline assessment was conducted in 2017 through semi-structured interviews and participatory sessions by using the Most Significant Change technique. Then the CSLCC team reviewed the main findings from the interviews and participatory sessions, and gave an endline score of each capacity area to the institutional stakeholders by using the inventory toolkit. The scoring result of each institution served as an endline score and was then compared
with its baseline value.

The data shared has been de-identified. Details of household head names, GPS locations, and phone numbers have been removed. New IDs have been assigned to each household using a unique code.

This data asset established the baseline levels and conditions of Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) services and behaviors in the USHA Northern cluster districts and provided a baseline against which to measure behavioral and service delivery changes over the life of the USHA Activity. It also generated a wealth index for populations in each of the target districts and assessed the percentage of the population in the lowest two poverty quintiles. The baseline survey instruments were designed using the current JMP/UNICEF household WASH questionnaire that is consistent with the requirements of the Sustainable Development Goal #6. Specifically, the survey includes questions about: 1) household assets to determine wealth quintiles per district, 2) current levels of household and community WASH services, and 3) behavioral practices related to WASH and resource allocation.

resource.name: Ghana Early Grade Math Pilot Impact Evaluation: Endline Pupil Data
resource.description: The Early Grade Math Pilot program in Ghana, implemented under the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) Partnership for Education Learning Activity, was evaluated with an independent randomized controlled trial between 2017 and 2018. This data asset contains the two waves of data collected in Ghana during this time period. This dataset contains survey pupil data from the activity endline.

domain_metadata.value: Social Impact. 2023. Ghana Early Grade Math Pilot Impact Evaluation: Endline Pupil Data. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/u73b-yrcp.

All data sets in this data asset have been comprehensively anonymized according to Social Impact procedures. Anonymization procedures included removing direct identifiers and removing or recoding indirect identifiers. These datasets were subsequently reviewed and approved for dissemination by Social Impact's internal Institutional Review Board.

This data asset contains detailed data from a total of four survey instruments, one classroom observation tool, and pupil scores on the EGRA and GENA assessments. This data was collected from 120 schools, 240 teachers, and 4,800 pupils. As such, this data asset contains substantial information regarding primary education in Ghana.

resource.name: Section L5 Food Security
resource.description: The survey interviewed 254 retailer shops in 10 sub-cities of Addis Ababa. 30 supermarkets, 20 mini-markets, 100 regular shops, 80 dairy shops and 24 open market shops selling dairy products were interviewed. Details of the sampling strategy is found in the attachment. The survey collected information on the characteristics of the shop, details of dairy products sold, prices and quality. Policy makers, research, and other stakeholders can use this data to analyses dairy value chain in Ethiopia and dairy retailing practices in Ethiopia. This data set was collected through research of the project “Improving the evidence and policies for better performing livestock systems in Ethiopia” lead by the International Food Policy Research Institution as part of the Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Livestock Systems.

resource.name: FTF Ghana 2015 Interim Population-Based Survey: Household Identification
resource.description: Feed the Future (FTF) initiative in Ghana is a collaborative effort that supports country-owned processes and plans for improving food security and nutrition, particularly in the northern part of the country. These datasets cover the interim survey that took place in 2015 and was designed as a follow-up to the baseline survey that happened from 2012 to 2013. The survey covered a range of indicators organized around four groups: (1) economic well-being; (2) women and children anthropometry; (3) hunger and diet diversity; and (4) women's empowerment. The survey design involved two stages in which enumeration areas were selected followed by households. Data was collected in a face-to-face fashion using well-designed questionnaires and other study materials.

domain_metadata.value: Kansas State University. 2019. FTF Ghana 2015 Interim Population-Based Survey: Household Identification. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/u8g4-kqxe.

Data elements with no reported value have been removed. Data elements that provide the same information in terms of detail have been removed and the most balanced element of these data elements have been kept. Latitude and longitude structure of GPS have been removed. Data elements that carry no information value for research questions involving these data such as survey administration related data elements have been removed.
Data covers a wide range of indicators and variables that were included in the survey.

resource.name: USAID Anticorruption Projects Database
resource.description: The Anticorruption Projects Database (Database) includes information about USAID projects with anticorruption interventions implemented worldwide between 2007 and 2013. The Database includes about 300 long-term country projects and regional or short-term projects. Projects were identified and information collected by the six Implementing Partners (IP) of the ENGAGE Indefinite Quantity Contract. Criteria for selecting projects included: distinctive project interventions targeted at reducing corruption or promoting government integrity, accountability and transparency that ultimately results in reducing opportunities to corruption. Availability of sufficient information about the projects was another criterion for selecting them to the Database. This included but was not limited to project description and results, implementation timeframe, project value, and implementer. After reviewing approximately 2000 projects, more than 300 were identified for the Database.

resource.name: Farm Plots Survey for Agriculture for Children's Empowerment (ACE) in Liberia- Fertilizer and Seed Baseline Dataset
resource.description:
The STRIVE project, funded by USAID's Displaced Children and Orphans Fund (DCOF) and managed by FHI 360, used market-led economic strengthening initiatives to improve the well-being of vulnerable children. Through STRIVE, ACDI/VOCA implemented the Agriculture for Children’s Empowerment (ACE) Project in Liberia, which is founded on the premise that increased household economic security will stimulate more consistent investments in children’s well being via longer term social investments in education and nutrition. ACE’s primary focus was on the horticulture value chain (VC) — the production and marketing of vegetables by smallholder farmers in Montserrado, Bong, and Nimba counties of Liberia. ACE also strengthened smallholder rice farming to increase household food security using a market-sensitive approach to rice seed lending and cultivation.
 
 This dataset contains baseline information about the fertilizer and seed used on each plot the household owns.

We have used the following steps to anonymize the datasets:1. Remove location variables such as county and Village and retain District 2. Use k-anonymity to mitigate the following variables sex, occupation, relationship to household head, education, dwelling characteristics, and District. To achieve the threshold of k=3, we will recode variables occupation, relationship to household head, education, dwelling characteristics, and District into broader categories 3. Aggregate or recode variables such as Age (into 10 years categories), diploma (any diploma above high school into other), and grade (into Primary, Junior High, and Senior High)4. Top code variables such as household size (15+ at baseline and 17+ at Endline) and rent paid. 5. Remove direct identifiers (names and cell phone numbers); remove probing variables such as Other-specify when they contain individuals’ names or reference to individuals with a status of refugee.

resource.name: Haiti Sorghum Intercropping Sugarcane Aphid Study 2018-2019 - Plant Measurements Dataset
resource.description: This dataset captures sorghum plant height and stem diameter. It contains 1,080 rows and 7 columns.  Two experiments were conducted, one planted on 8/22/2018 (fall 2018) and another planted on 1/19/2019 (spring 2019), in Jonc-Labeille, Haiti. Three experimental treatments were compared: sorghum, sorghum intercropped with maize, and sorghum intercropped with pigeon pea. The sorghum variety was “Bout gode,” the maize variety was “Chicken corn,” and the pigeon pea was “Pwa kongo local.” A randomized complete block design experiment was used.

We identified variables within the asset that present privacy risk (key variables) and applied a 3-anonymity technique on categorical key variables, such as county, sex and age group. In order to reach the 3-anonymity threshold, we recoded some variables and suppressed values that increased the risk of re-identification. Doing so reduces the precision of the cells, while preserving statistical utility. 3-anonymity mitigates risk on key categorical variables in a combined way.
Data were collected for a wide range of variables to better inform the design of the project and could potentially be reused to plan additional projects in the same sectors in other regions.

resource.name: Rift Valley Fever Innovation Lab: Vaccination of livestock, subcutaneous with MP-12 and MP-12-NSm-del2
resource.description:
Subcutaneous needle vaccination against Rift Valley fever virus (RVFV): Antibody response for goats,sheep and calves vaccinated with MP12 and MP12Nsm del vaccines analysed by PRNT 80% and commercial cELISAkit. cELISA results are expressed in inhibition percent (S/N%) and PRNT results in reciprocal of PRNT 80% neutralization titers. The overall purpose of the Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Rift Valley Fever Control in Agriculture is to increase the food supply by developing and applying a vaccine for the prevention of Rift Valley fever disease among livestock in Africa.  Rift Valley Fever (RVF) is a mosquito-borne viral disease that continues to have a devastating impact on human and animal health in Africa.  Since the discovery of RVF as the cause of an outbreak among sheep and humans during the early 1930s in the Rift Valley in Kenya, the disease has emerged as one of the most important zoonoses in Africa. The disease has and continues to affect the health of thousands to millions of humans and animals, and the livestock industry has lost millions of dollars, and therefore, affecting hundreds of millions of those whose livelihood depends on livestock, exaggerating poverty on already deprived communities.
Full dataset available in the file: Livestock_vaccinated_with_MP-12_MP-12_NSm-del_SubQ_Salekwa.xlsx

resource.description:
This data set contains biological information from important coastal mangrove areas situated at the border of, or near the targeted seascapes of the Caribbean Marine Biodiversity Program (CMBP). The data covers: raw species density, diameter at breast height, canopy cover and average heights; GIS data on all locations where data was collected.
Targeted seascapes and corresponding countries include:
1) The Mangroves of Bajo Yuna and Los Corozos - Samana Bay - Dominican Republic
2) The Mangroves of Protected Area of Three Bays - Haiti

This file reports density data on mangroves of Bajo Yuna and Los Corozos in Samana Bay, Dominican Republic.  The two datasets, "data" and "density" together describe each area.

The overall objective of the USAID Caribbean Marine Biodiversity Program (CMBP) is to reduce threats to marine-coastal biodiversity in priority areas in the Caribbean—including high biodiversity ecosystems such as coral reefs, mangroves, and seagrass beds—to achieve sustained biodiversity conservation, maintain critical ecosystem services, and realize tangible improvements in human wellbeing for communities adjacent to marine managed areas (MMAs). To achieve this objective, the CMBP addresses direct and indirect threats to marine and coastal biodiversity at multiple geographic scales simultaneously. More specifically, the CMBP includes nested and inter-connected actions across four geographic scales: site, seascape, national and regional. Most of the funding and activities are centered on four targeted seascapes: North Coast of Hispaniola (focus on Haiti); Samaná Bay (Dominican Republic);(iii) Pedro Bank and Southwest Coast of Jamaica (Jamaica)(iv) Grenadine Bank (Grenada and St. Vincent and the Grenadines).

resource.name: Feed the Future Tajikistan Zone of Influence Population Based Survey, Women's Empowerment in Agriculture Index-Household File
resource.description: The baseline survey in Tajikistan captures data in the Feed the Future Zones of Influence (ZOI), comprised of 12 of the 24 districts in Khatlon province. A total of 2,000 households in the ZOI were surveyed for the PBS data collection activity. These households are spread across 100 standard enumeration areas in the targeted districts. The survey is comprised of ten CSV files: a children's file, a household-level file, a household member level file, a women's file, several files describing consumption, and two files used to construct the Women's Empowerment in Agriculture Index.  This file reports household level data from the Women's Empowerment in Agriculture Index (WEAI). The WEAI measures the empowerment, agency, and inclusion of women in the agriculture sector in an effort to identify and address the constraints that limit women’s full engagement in the agriculture sector.

resource.name: Program Evaluation of USAID/Uganda SUSTAIN Activity: Regional Referral Hospital Staff Data
resource.description:
USAID/Uganda’s Strengthening Uganda’s Systems for Treating AIDS Nationally (SUSTAIN) activity supports Uganda’s Ministry of Health (MOH) to strengthen quality and comprehensive HIV/AIDS care, prevention, laboratory and tuberculosis (TB) services at selected regional referral and district health care facilities in Uganda, as well as build the capacity of the public health system to sustain these services. SUSTAIN is a six­-year USAID­-funded activity launched in 2010 and implemented by University Research Co., LLC (URC). SUSTAIN is one of many PEPFAR-­funded activities to address the HIV/AIDS epidemic in Uganda. The main objective of the SUSTAIN program evaluation was to examine the activity’s methodology for achieving its
objectives in order to inform future USAID design work. USAID noted that URC had performed well on SUSTAIN, as evidenced by its activity reports, but wanted an evaluation of the approach used by SUSTAIN to inform future program designs. SUSTAIN implementation adapted to contextual changes in the Government of Uganda's (GoU) HIV/AIDS strategy responding to a spike in new infections and people living with HIV, and major shifts in PEPFAR policy.

domain_metadata.value: President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR)
Panagora Group. 2020. Program Evaluation of USAID/Uganda SUSTAIN Activity: Regional Referral Hospital Staff Data. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/uxhj-45pn.
Although the evaluators did identify participants in the focus groups and key informant interviews, the data that could identify respondents was not included in any of the spreadsheets.

The dataset consists of recorded responses to a series of questions asked during key informant interviews (KII) or client focus groups regarding the delivery of HIV/AIDS related services. There are 11 spreadsheets, each recording the answers of a different set of actors in health service delivery: district health officers, focus groups comprised of clients (two spreadsheets), clinic staff, laboratory staff, implementing partners, lower level facility staff, Ministry of Health staff, regional referral hospital staff, SUSTAIN project staff, and USAID staff.

resource.name: Collecting Taxes Database 2020-2021 - Performance Data
resource.description:
USAID's Collecting Taxes Database (CTD) is a compilation of international statistics about taxation designed to provide policymakers, practitioners, and researchers with the means to conduct analysis on domestic revenue mobilization (DRM). It is part of a wider agenda of the international community to help countries strengthen their tax systems and mobilize domestic revenue.

The CTD includes information on tax performance and tax administration variables for 200 countries and territories. USAID plans to update the CTD annually.

The CTD comprises a set of 30 indicators divided into three main categories -- (1) Tax
Rates and Structure; (2) Tax Performance; and (3) Tax Administration -- and includes
information on 200 national tax systems. The tax rates and structure indicators capture
historical tax rates and thresholds. The tax performance indicators measure how
effectively the tax system produces revenues.

The CTD Performance Data includes Tax Rates and Structure and Tax Performance data.

resource.name: Protecting Human Rights (PHR) Program: Number of Child Marriages Prevented Dataset
resource.description: This asset contains disaggregated data on the prevented child marriages in Bangladesh by location. The Protecting Human Rights (PHR) Program works to reduce domestic violence, child marriage and related human rights abuses in 102 unions under eight upazilas of six districts. With support from USAID from March 2011 to March 2017, PHR was implemented by Plan International Bangladesh, the Bangladesh National Women Lawyers’ Association and 11 local NGOs. PHR uses an integrated and broad­-based approach that includes advocacy, capacity building, access to justice, services for survivors, and mass awareness and educational projects.

domain_metadata.value: Plan International USA. 2020. Protecting Human Rights (PHR) Program: Number of Child Marriages Prevented Dataset. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/v78w-twpa.

resource.name: Mangrove Monitoring Density Data: Mangroves of Protected Area of Three Bays, Haiti
resource.description:
This data set contains biological information from important coastal mangrove areas situated at the border of, or near the targeted seascapes of the Caribbean Marine Biodiversity Program (CMBP). The data covers: raw species density, diameter at breast height, canopy cover and average heights; GIS data on all locations where data was collected.
Targeted seascapes and corresponding countries include:
1) The Mangroves of Bajo Yuna and Los Corozos - Samana Bay - Dominican Republic
2) The Mangroves of Protected Area of Three Bays - Haiti

This file reports density data on mangroves of the Protected Area of Three Bays, Haiti.  The two datasets, "data" and "density" together describe each area.

The overall objective of the USAID Caribbean Marine Biodiversity Program (CMBP) is to reduce threats to marine-coastal biodiversity in priority areas in the Caribbean—including high biodiversity ecosystems such as coral reefs, mangroves, and seagrass beds—to achieve sustained biodiversity conservation, maintain critical ecosystem services, and realize tangible improvements in human wellbeing for communities adjacent to marine managed areas (MMAs). To achieve this objective, the CMBP addresses direct and indirect threats to marine and coastal biodiversity at multiple geographic scales simultaneously. More specifically, the CMBP includes nested and inter-connected actions across four geographic scales: site, seascape, national and regional. Most of the funding and activities are centered on four targeted seascapes: North Coast of Hispaniola (focus on Haiti); Samaná Bay (Dominican Republic);(iii) Pedro Bank and Southwest Coast of Jamaica (Jamaica)(iv) Grenadine Bank (Grenada and St. Vincent and the Grenadines).

resource.description: The baseline survey in Tajikistan captures data in the Feed the Future Zones of Influence (ZOI), comprised of 12 of the 24 districts in Khatlon province. This file reports survey results related to households.

resource.name: Program Evaluation of USAID/Uganda SUSTAIN Activity: Focus Group Data
resource.description:
USAID/Uganda’s Strengthening Uganda’s Systems for Treating AIDS Nationally (SUSTAIN) activity supports Uganda’s Ministry of Health (MOH) to strengthen quality and comprehensive HIV/AIDS care, prevention, laboratory and tuberculosis (TB) services at selected regional referral and district health care facilities in Uganda, as well as build the capacity of the public health system to sustain these services. SUSTAIN is a six­-year USAID­-funded activity launched in 2010 and implemented by University Research Co., LLC (URC). SUSTAIN is one of many PEPFAR-­funded activities to address the HIV/AIDS epidemic in Uganda. The main objective of the SUSTAIN program evaluation was to examine the activity’s methodology for achieving its
objectives in order to inform future USAID design work. USAID noted that URC had performed well on SUSTAIN, as evidenced by its activity reports, but wanted an evaluation of the approach used by SUSTAIN to inform future program designs. SUSTAIN implementation adapted to contextual changes in the Government of Uganda's (GoU) HIV/AIDS strategy responding to a spike in new infections and people living with HIV, and major shifts in PEPFAR policy.

domain_metadata.value: President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR)
Panagora Group. 2020. Program Evaluation of USAID/Uganda SUSTAIN Activity: Focus Group Data. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/vcba-gkfh.
Although the evaluators did identify participants in the focus groups and key informant interviews, the data that could identify respondents was not included in any of the spreadsheets.

The dataset consists of recorded responses to a series of questions asked during key informant interviews (KII) or client focus groups regarding the delivery of HIV/AIDS related services. There are 11 spreadsheets, each recording the answers of a different set of actors in health service delivery: district health officers, focus groups comprised of clients (two spreadsheets), clinic staff, laboratory staff, implementing partners, lower level facility staff, Ministry of Health staff, regional referral hospital staff, SUSTAIN project staff, and USAID staff.

resource.description:
This dataset contains information about the characteristics of the household’s largest maize field. The table can be combined with other datasets in this data asset using the 'hhid' column.

The purpose of collecting these data was to examine farm expansion and labor markets in rural Tanzania. Data were collected in 8 rural districts of Tanzania: Mvomero, Kilombero, Njombe, Kiteto, Magu, Moshi Rural, Mkuranga and Liwale.

The data were collected through the Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Food Security Policy (FSP).

resource.name: Baseline Study of Food for Peace Title II Development Food Assistance Program in Niger--Agricultural Practices: Section 1
resource.description: This dataset describes the agricultural practices within households interviewed as part of Baseline Study of Food for Peace Title II Development Food Assistance Program in the Maradi and Zinder regions in Niger. In fiscal year 2012, USAID's Office of Food for Peace (FFP) awarded funding to private voluntary organizations (PVOs) to design and implement a multi-year Title II development food assistance program in Niger. The main purpose of the Title II program is to improve long-term food security of chronically food insecure population in the target regions. FFP contracted a firm, ICF International to conduct a baseline study in targeted areas of the country prior to the start of the new program.  The purpose of the study was to assess the current status of key indicators, have a better understanding of prevailing conditions and perceptions of the population in the implementation areas, and serve as a point of comparison for future final evaluations.  Results would also be used to further refine program targeting and, where possible, to understand the relationship between variables to inform program design.  The study was conducted in 2013, while FFP expects to conduct final evaluations as close as possible to the end of the program five years later. In the process of migrating data to the current DDL platform, datasets with a large number of variables required splitting into multiple spreadsheets.  They should be reassembled by the user to understand the data fully.
